t: 2113. Elements in Array After Removing and Replacing Elements
o: The array cycles with period 2n: n minutes of removals from the front, then n minutes of appends restoring the original order. During the removal phase (minute t, 0 <= t < n) the array is nums[t..n-1], so index i exists only if i < n-t. During the append phase (n <= t < 2n) the first t-n elements have been restored, so index i exists only if i < t-n. Example 1: at t=2 the array is [2] so index 0 gives 2; at t=3 the array is empty so anything returns -1; at t=5 the array is [0,1] so index 0 gives 0. With n <= 100 and up to 1e5 queries, either precomputing all 2n states or answering each query with O(1) arithmetic both work easily.
k: The whole process is periodic with period 2n, so reduce time modulo 2n.
In phase 1 the available prefix length is n-t; in phase 2 it is t-n — index i is valid iff i < that length.

a.i: Simulate one full cycle and snapshot the array after every minute. Each query then reduces to a lookup at minute t mod 2n.
s: Simulate 2n-1 steps: for t <= n remove the front, otherwise append nums[t-n-1], storing a copy after each step.
For each query take states[t mod 2n] and return index i if it exists, else -1.
a.t: O(n^2 + q) — building 2n snapshots of up to n elements dominates

a.i: No simulation is needed: minute t mod 2n directly tells you which contiguous slice of nums is visible, and its length is n-t in phase 1 or t-n in phase 2.
s: If t < n the visible slice is nums[t..n-1] (length n-t); otherwise it is nums[0..t-n-1] (length t-n).
Answer nums[i] if i is below that length, else -1.
a.t: O(q) — constant work per query after reducing t modulo 2n

w: Use the O(1) formula in an interview; the snapshot method is a good sanity check. Pitfalls: forgetting the modulo (times can exceed 2n), and off-by-one on when appends start (at minute n the array is empty, first append lands at minute n+1). Follow-up: what if times were up to 1e18 — the modulo handles it unchanged.
